The reality is that the vast majority of families are homeless or housing-insecure, at least here in greater Boston, because of economic conditions, domestic violence, and multi-generational systemic racism. comments.body: Now out of China, I often wonder: How can it be that a proud, nuclear-armed world power is scared of red ink?  The answer is the state apparatus is afraid because they do not feel legitimate and they do not have the support of the people.   The original legitimacy of the communist party came from the 1949 land campaign,  and the iron rice bowl, and the constant propaganda and agitation for the workers and peasants,  they dissipated their legitimacy in the famines, the great leap forward and cultural revoltuon, this was replaced with a strong and growing economy and non involvement in poltics by the people, the party provided wealth and opportunity and controlled politics,  now this has collapsed and all that is left is coercion and surveillance and inertia  the partys legitimacy has collapsed again.

comments.name: OnceOverseasProf
comments.body: The Chinese Communist Party leadership has always been insecure, striving to maintain its legitimacy at every turn. But the fact that the slogan "Serve the People," epitomized by Lei Feng in the early 1960s, continues to bring smirks to the faces of the older masses who appreciate its bitter irony speaks volumes. Hooligan writer Wang Shuo once satirized the Party for being uncool in the1990s, at the moment when it was the most relaxed, as Higgins noted. Now the Xi regime makes no pretense of its return to Marxist nationalism, as former Australian leader Kevin Rudd has amply described in his recent book about Xi. I was there during the period from 1997 to 2010 when things were truly opening up. But when I returned in mid-2012, the tone of the greeting to university personnel by the local Party boss in Zhejiang to mark the opening of an American university satellite campus in Zhejiang was more ominous than inviting. The fact that Xi had been governor and Party secretary in this province just a short time ago was also ironic. Then in 2018, I returned for a two-week visit with old friends in Beijing. Now a megapolis, the capital had lost much of its charm. Traffic congestion abounded. Long gone were the legions of bicyclists and the mazes of back alleys. Like Higgins, I made note of the omnipresence of surveillance cameras and felt ill at ease. My goal to return to China to teach was nixed by the new age restrictions for obtaining a Z work visa. I felt a sense of sadness and loss

comments.name: AR
comments.body:
An unfortunate flat report lacking in any real insight into China or nuances of life and opinion.

Yes, it is a repressive regime against the people of China (although that reporter seemed more miffed about foreign reporters). US spy agencies using reporters as assets and propaganda outlets, has hurt press freedom, as there is naturally suspicion and hostility.

Given the hostility and threats by the United States, I wouldn't dismiss the Chinese attitude as paranoid. The United States has surrounded China with military bases, weapons, and endless provocations, and an undeniably hostile rhetoric. I don't recall the last time China threatened to annihilate another country, people and civilization, unlike the United States. 

The government is concerned about the deepening economic crisis leading to political restiveness and dissent. Obviously the spying reflects their fears about people's anger at unemployment, low wages, loss of savings, consumer goods inflation at the same time there is inflation. Too bad we didn't learn about that.

The writer comes across as incurious, with a grudge and a score to settle, not an observer. When I was in China I had many interesting conversations about myriad topics. But I didn't start by asking their opinions on the Chinese government. 

It would have been interesting to learn their thoughts about the war on Iran, AI, population declines in China and the region, developments in Chinese culture, prospects for youth and the elderly, and more.

The sapphire stone in the engagement ring brought back a sad memory for me. When we got engaged, my husband bought me a beautiful gold engagement ring with an emerald cut center stone held in place by four gold prongs. It had diamond baguettes flanking the left and right side of the diamond. My wedding ring was a solid gold band as was his.
On our 25th wedding anniversary I ran several errands to three different places: the post office, the grocery store and finally, my doctor's office to make an appointment. I was certain the center diamond (1.50 carats)was in place until I got to the doctor where I discovered it was missing. I was stunned. When I left the doctor, I retraced all my steps everywhere I had been but it was nowhere. I went home and virtually tore the inside of my car apart, moving all floor mats, all electric seats, climbing under and over every inch of the car interior and compartments. I even checked the trunk although I hadn't opened it.
I kept looking for it for days but it was gone. I filed a claim with my insurance company and our jeweler replaced it with a beautiful identical diamond. I wore it a few days later when we went to Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket and then to Newport, Rhode Island for our anniversary trip and kept checking it to be sure it was solid. We enjoyed our trip nevertheless.
Now I wear it infrequently because I don't want to lose it again. I get the prongs checked by our jeweler regularly.

comments.body:
My mother and aunt, both painters, regarded Piero as one of the greats, along with Matisse, Picasso, Michelangelo, and he was their personal favorite.  

On our only trip to Italy (1989) we went to Arezzzo from Florence to see the magnificent mural (to fully appreciate his mastery I'd suggest an art book with detailed photos of some backgrounds, small masterpieces of few brushstrokes).  

Inspired by that, on a whim we jumped into our car and made a memorably beautiful drive along Tuscan country roads to San Sepulchro, arriving about an hour before the museum closed.  

"The Resurrection" hit me like a ton of bricks.  We saw a lot of art on that trip--Naples, Rome, Florence, Milan--but that moment is the one that sticks in my memory.  I'm not much religious, but that painting makes a convincing case that Jesus is God.

Piero could do anything, and do it economically, but what's beyond adjectives is his portraiture.  Spend some time meditating on the faces of his subjects, and you may see what I mean.

I lived in a rural northern California county for ten years and was active for a time in helping my community, CALFIRE (the state's firefighting agency), and several UC-Berkeley associated scientists deal with the rising tide of wildfire in the state.
This is what I learned, and why I decided eight years ago to move as far away as possible from that beautiful, but wildfire-prone state.
Early detection is indeed helpful as this article chronicles. Small fires are much easier to put out (and remain out) than larger ones.
The group I helped focused on satelite-based detection but its technology and timing parameters were not well-suited to early detection in many instances.
This is why I recommended a terrestrial approach for northen California which I don't believe was covered by the early spotting system portrayed in this article at the time. Some small-scale experiments were done but nothing like what is now being done across the state. This is a major improvement over what was available at the time a major wildfire tore through my former community destroying 1300 homes nearby and thousands more across the county.
But early detection, while helpful, is not the only action that determines whether a fire is caught early or spreads.
The affected community must evacuate quickly for CALFIRE to stop the spread of wildfire, and as several recent fires show, this often doesn't happen quickly enough.
Communities should focus some of their effort on evacuation planning and practice.

Isn't "getting paid to complain" an oxymoron?

Money (assuming that that is the payment type expected) has no bearing upon nor value-formative influence toward expression of one's ideas--even when sometimes they take the form of complaint.

Further, I view "Letters to the Editor" as a forum inviting of freedom of expression of the content and tone of one's thoughts, feelings, and existential impressions on a specific topic--not only a sense of "complaint".

Public comment need not always be cast in an antagonistic light; on the contrary, the spirit inherent to "Letters to the Editor" seems to invite a furtherance of light being shed on a detailed viewpoint or subject, one that enhances dialogue because it is based on intelligence--the thoughts expressed there may actually be offered in a spirit of embellishment of the original story ideas--finding areas to be furthered by another's perspective.

In this dreary current age of constant  contention, disagreement, antagonism  and war--"Letters to the Editor" could be looked to for serious engagement with strong ideas and approaches which positively sustain our social dialogue--certainly one more favorable in enhancement of this thing called thought.

Thank you for this terrific piece of writing. Here in formerly-soggy western Washington, my husband and I came close to losing our home in 2020 when a storm-felled tree sparked a fire on our partially wooded acreage. Of course, we'd known about climate change for years and accepted its reality, but that was the year that it really hit home, as I stood in the ashes at once thankful our home was spared and weeping for our beautiful trees that had been torched and scarred. Living on this piece of land for over 35 years, we've witnessed the changes with our own eyes--the hotter, drier, longer summers; the now-regular periods where we're steeped in smoke. We've tried to prepare and adapt--installing a heat pump to cool our home, implementing fire-safe measures, purchasing HEPA air purifiers, keeping go-bags ready.

But you can only prepare and adapt so much, and I often find myself succumbing to hopelessness as the climate continues to heat and the fires burn ever hotter and the greedy, powerful climate deniers running our country continue to spread their lies and strive to undo every bit of environmental progress that we've made. And to know--with such a deep, burning sickness and shame--that a majority of people in our country voted for this. 

I wonder, when they're all grown up and living a climate nightmare, what our children and grandchildren will think of us?

But, none of things, at scale, are going to happen soon enough.

To quote one of the major thinkers of our time:

“No problem is so big or so complicated that it can’t be run away from.” Linus van Pelt.

If you live in, or near, a fire-adapted ecosystem, sell your house and move. Do it now.

I remember when AIDS was just starting.  I remember the ignorant statements from President Reagan and the less than charitable statements and condemnations from some well known preachers.  None of that helped things.  The same can be said of what former Governor Christie did when there was an earlier outbreak of Ebola in Africa and Americans were exposed or cared for patients there.  

When we help our neighbors we do help ourselves.  We live in a country that can afford to contribute to world health.  Yes, we have a lousy health care system. comments.name: Mark Kropf
comments.body:
The story here is among the most important ones that people can read.

So much of our Science, especially in a time of AI and of conspiracy theories must be understood for the difficulties of understanding of what a true situation may be.

My career in Medicine has shown that things are true until they aren't.  They often resemble the truth, but concepts change over time.

The notion that Dr. Piot faced that Infectious Disease was a settled area for research now strikes us for how ridiculous it truly was in its time!

Simplistic thinking is there for most any person coming to look at how we understand what is about us.

In my 70+ years, I have been impressed how many mistakes are made to get to answers which remain mostly imperfect approximations of some level of truth.

The iterative nature of understanding is extremely important, and not merely for Ebola's filovirus nature, but also for most any other area. 

AI will hardly solve all problems as it supplies 'the answer' to us.   We need to learn that we NEARLY NEVER have a complete answer!

As so many people are convinced that they know Autism is caused by immunizations (virtually impossible!), we see what having absolute certainty or trusting absolute knowledge can be dangerous.

What we know of Ebola or Measles will be refined in the future, but mostly we are on the right track!

There is nothing wrong with saying I don't know or holding out for the most likely answer while leaving the mind open to some other explanation.

I often bicycle through parts of this House district -- which has a diverse (divided?) demographic.  One that makes this an interesting race.

On the east side, bordering the Hudson River sit very "blue" Piermont and bluish Nyack.  Yet westwards, centered around Orangeburg and Tappan you find a much more conservative population.  One comprised in part of current and retired NYC police and firefighters. 

A glimpse of political lawn signs informs you that east of State Route 340 Conley is strong.  But cross that road and the Lawler signs are ubiqitous.

Nonetheless, Conley's military background does complicate this race.  It's not usual for a Democrat to tout military experience.  I don't doubt that Democrats will be unbothered by this background.  So the question is whether that experience will entice the District's more conservative voters, who often have a military past themselves, to consider Conley as one of their own and vote for her?

Recently re-read Berger's "Portraits," and it vividly reminded me of two things: (1) he was an enormously talented individual; and (2) in his essays he can bend toward the tendentious. Akin to, say, Graham Greene when it came to his myopia toward the USSR and against the U.S.

Berger can lose himself in his own voice: he wrote a lot, frequently short reviews of this or that artist, and while said artist no doubt appreciated the review, the artist in question sometimes loses out to Berger's lyrical shenanigans. 

Or worse: His chapter in *Portraits* on Käthe Kollwitz mentions her only once briefly at the beginning, and then he spends the entire essay lauding an art administrator friend of his in Dresden. From Berger's political standpoint, Käthe Kollwitz should have been a prize!

Read him, value him, don't mindlessly apotheosize him.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
There are people who can do this--

--and heaven knows, I'm not one of them.  

People who stroll into museums and spend ten or fifteen minutes or half an hour or an hour--

--staring at a single painting.  A still life, maybe, or a portrait of someone who died in 1890.  And they discern everything.  All the shadings, the nuances.  The subtleties.  Everything. 

How I wish I could accompany such persons.  Hear what they had to say--

--and here Mr. Berger was exactly that sort of man.  And he had so much to say.  And people hung on every word.  

I've known writers (notably Nabokov) with extraordinarily sensitive eyes.  Writers who (when describing something) miss nothing.  A rare gift--

--and Mr. Berger was obviously one of these.  But with a difference.  He was excruciatingly alive to the human beings he was looking at.  What their lives were like--their joys, their sorrows--

--and the ineffable sang froid with which society was letting them down.  And he put it all down in black and white--

--and kept putting it down!

--till as they say, the Grim Reaper came calling--

--and we're left with those incredibly voluminous writings.  

" For Death, he taketh all away, but them he cannot take."  

No.  Not those writings.  Not a chance!

Thanks, NYT.

comments.name: C Clark
comments.body: I have read several of John Berger's books but can only claim real familiarity with one, "A fortunate Man", his photo-essay of an English country doctor. Accompanied by Jean Mohr's photos, it is the best and most nuanced assessment of the complexities, challenges  and rewards of providing ethical medical care I have ever come across.
